title: How to Become an SBA Lender: Requirements, Capital, and the Approval Path
summary: Become an SBA lender with a regulator, enough capital, and full loan operations. Banks have the fastest path; SBLCs need $5M+.
body_markdown:
### How to Become an SBA Lender: Requirements, Capital, and the Approval Path


### What It Takes to Become an SBA Lender


To become an SBA lender, get supervised by a federal regulator, an SBA-satisfactory state regulator, or SBA itself as an SBLC or NFRL. Then hold sufficient capital, serve the public, meet character standards, and show you can evaluate, process, close, disburse, service, liquidate, and litigate loans. The U.S. Small Business Administration says on[SBA's lender program page](https://www.sba.gov/sba-lenders/) to start by contacting a lender relations specialist at your local district office.


The payoff is a federal guaranty on standard 7(a) loans. SBA guarantees up to 85% on loans of $150,000 or less and up to 75% above that, under 13 CFR 120.210. The maximum 7(a) loan is $5 million, per 13 CFR 120.151.


Demand is real. The U.S. Small Business Administration reported a record FY2025 in[SBA's Siemens SBLC announcement](https://legacy.sba.gov/article/2026/06/17/sba-approves-siemens-financial-services-7a-lender) : $45 billion guaranteed to 85,000 small businesses via 7(a) and 504. SBA said that volume ran through a network of over 4,300 lenders.


Treat approval as two tests at once. One is regulatory—who supervises you and how much capital you hold. The other is operational—whether you can carry a loan from intake to liquidation.


### Choose Your Path: Bank, SBLC, Community Advantage, or Broker


Your entry path decides who examines you, how much capital you hold, and what the timeline looks like. Banks and credit unions already have a regulator. Non-banks need SBA as their supervisor, or a partner model that skips the license entirely.


Path Who it fits Supervisor Capital standard Current status


Regulated bank or credit union Depository institutions with an existing regulator Federal Financial Institution Regulator or SBA-satisfactory state banking regulator "Adequately capitalized" counts as sufficient Start with your SBA district office


SBLC Non-bank lenders, including fintechs, seeking a direct license SBA only Greater of $5M or 10% of share of outstanding loans Moratorium lifted May 12, 2023; applications open only when SBA publishes a Federal Register notice


Community Advantage SBLC Mission-focused lenders SBA Set at SBA's discretion, plus a loan loss reserve SBA reinstated a moratorium on new licenses (as of May 2025)


Broker or platform Platforms offering SBA loans without lending No SBA license; operates as an Agent under 13 CFR 103 No SBA capital minimum Agent fees disclosed on SBA Form 159


### Regulated Banks and Credit Unions


Banks and credit unions have the shortest path. Under 13 CFR 120.410, they qualify through supervision by a Federal Financial Institution Regulator or a state banking regulator satisfactory to SBA. If your regulator rates you "adequately capitalized," SBA treats that as sufficient permanent capital.


### Small Business Lending Companies (SBLCs)


SBLCs are non-bank lenders licensed by SBA. SBA's[SBLC moratorium rescission rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/04/12/2023-07181/small-business-lending-company-sblc-moratorium-rescission-and-removal-of-the-requirement-for-a-loan) , published in the Federal Register, lifted the moratorium on licensing new SBLCs effective May 12, 2023. The same rule states that SBLCs are regulated, supervised, and examined solely by SBA.


Licensing isn't continuous—SBA accepts applications only when it publishes a Federal Register notice. There is precedent for new entrants. SBA announced in June 2026 that Siemens Small Business Lending had won an SBLC license, calling it one of 16 approved non-bank SBA lenders.


Non-Federally Regulated Lenders (NFRLs) are a second non-bank route under SOP 50 56, with a separate capital rule. For fintechs and platforms, both routes mean SBA exams, a capital floor, and discretionary approval.


### Community Advantage SBLCs


SBA created Community Advantage SBLCs in 2023 as a mission-focused SBLC type. Their capital is set at SBA's discretion, plus a required loan loss reserve.


The U.S. Small Business Administration's[Community Advantage moratorium announcement](https://legacy.sba.gov/article/2025/05/19/sba-overhauls-reckless-biden-era-lending-program) of May 19, 2025, said SBA had reinstated the moratorium on new Community Advantage lending licenses. Treat that as the status as of May 2025, and confirm the current position with SBA before planning around it.


### Preferred Lender Program (PLP) Status


PLP status is a later designation that SBA grants in its discretion—you can't enter the program with it. Under 13 CFR 120.450, PLP lenders process, close, service, and liquidate SBA loans with reduced documentation and prior-approval requirements.


Approved lenders sign a Supplemental Guarantee Agreement with a term of up to two years. Lenders with under three years of SBA lending experience get one year or less, per 13 CFR 120.440.


### Meet SBA Eligibility and Supervision Standards


13 CFR 120.410 sets the baseline every participating lender must meet, whatever the path. Expect SBA to test each requirement at approval and keep testing it afterward.


### Core Eligibility Requirements


- **Continuing ability:** Show you can evaluate, process, close, disburse, service, liquidate, and litigate small business loans.
- **Public access:** Be open to the public rather than operate as a financing subsidiary of an affiliate.
- **Character:** Meet the good character and ethics standards in 13 CFR 120.140.
- **Good standing:** Stay in good standing with SBA and with your state or federal regulator.


SBA also weighs performance. eCFR, the authoritative but unofficial online CFR, lists the[requirements for participating lenders](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-13/chapter-I/part-120/subpart-D/subject-group-ECFRc92e890a0eca5cc/section-120.410) , including satisfactory SBA performance "as determined by SBA in its discretion."


### Regulatory Supervision and Safe-and-Sound Operations


Every lender must be supervised and examined by a Federal Financial Institution Regulator, an SBA-satisfactory state banking regulator, or SBA. You must also stay in good standing with that supervisor.


You need to operate in a safe and sound condition, too. That means commercially reasonable lending policies, procedures, and standards of the kind prudent lenders use.


### Hold the Required Capital


Capital rules depend on your lender type. Banks lean on their existing regulatory status, while non-banks face a hard floor.


Lender type Minimum capital standard Source


Bank or credit union "Adequately capitalized" status counts as sufficient permanent capital 13 CFR 120.410


SBLC Greater of $5,000,000 or 10% of its share of outstanding loans (since Jan. 4, 2024) 13 CFR 120.471


Community Advantage SBLC Set at SBA's discretion, plus a loan loss reserve 13 CFR 120.471


NFRL Greater of the state minimum or $2,500,000 13 CFR 120.462


Per eCFR's[SBLC minimum capital rules](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-13/chapter-I/part-120/subpart-D/subject-group-ECFR13a0216058cc515/section-120.471) (13 CFR 120.471), the SBLC floor is $5,000,000 or 10% of its loan share, whichever is greater. That is a minimum, and SBA can set a higher requirement for an individual SBLC.


Only certain forms of capital count toward the SBLC minimum:


- **Equity:** Common stock, plus noncumulative preferred stock with no maturity date.
- **Paid-in and retained capital:** Additional paid-in capital and retained earnings of the business.
- **Nonprofit and pass-through capital:** Unrestricted net assets for nonprofits, plus LLC or LP contributions not repayable at a set time.


Capital also locks in place. Without SBA approval, an SBLC can't voluntarily reduce capital, repurchase more than 2% of its stock, or issue securities.


### Build the Operations SBA Expects


The "continuing ability" standard is operational—SBA tests whether you can carry a loan from intake to liquidation. Skip headcount-heavy builds—use data orchestration, decisioning, and document automation to meet it.

### Servicing, Liquidation, and Performance Monitoring


Lendflow's embedded finance customers operate with 80% smaller teams while converting similar funding volumes. Lean teams matter most after closing, when servicing work piles up.


Servicing and liquidation sit on the same requirement list as origination. SBA assigns a Risk Rating on a 1-to-5 scale, and 13 CFR 120.10 defines 1, 2, or 3 as acceptable.


SBA determines satisfactory performance in its discretion, weighing measures such as default, purchase, and loss rates. It publishes no numeric cutoffs, so map your[SBA loan servicing workflows](https://www.lendflow.com/post/sba-loan-servicing-how-it-works-for-borrowers-and-lenders) and monitoring before the first guaranty request.


### Step-by-Step: How to Apply for SBA Lender Approval


Here's how to become an SBA lender in six steps. Order matters, because each step depends on the one before it.


1. **Pick your path:** Choose bank, SBLC, or NFRL, and confirm your regulator status.
2. **Run a readiness check:** Test capital, credit policies, and staff SBA lending experience against 13 CFR 120.410.
3. **Contact SBA:** Reach a lender relations specialist at your local SBA district office.
4. **File a Lender Assessment Plan (non-banks):** SBLC and NFRL applicants submit one when SBA has an open application window. If invited, file a full application.
5. **Execute agreements and connect systems:** Sign your SBA agreements and set up CAFS access to submit guaranty requests through E-Tran.
6. **Build a track record:** Build performance history before you request PLP delegated authority.


For non-banks, SBA can approve or deny an application in its sole discretion. If your plan isn't advanced, you wait at least 6 months to resubmit; after a denial, you wait 12 months.


Step 5 is where tech onboarding starts. See our guide to[SBA E-Tran API integration](https://www.lendflow.com/post/sba-e-tran-api-integration-practical-guide-for-lenders-and-fintech-teams) for the practical setup.


### Lender or Broker: Which Model Fits Your Business


In the last 12 months, $1.5B+ in offers were made on Lendflow's platform (as of March 2025). You can offer SBA loans without holding a license yourself.


Per eCFR's[SBA agent definitions](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-13/chapter-I/part-103/section-103.1) in 13 CFR 103.1, a Referral Agent "identifies and refers an Applicant to a lender or a lender to an Applicant." A Lender Service Provider carries out lender functions for a lender, and SBA decides LSP status loan by loan.


Our[lender service provider rules](https://www.lendflow.com/post/sba-lender-service-provider-what-it-is-the-rules-and-how-lenders-scale-with-one) guide explains how lenders scale with one. Agent fees go on SBA Form 159, one form per Agent, and SBA does not allow contingency fees. Those details reflect the 2018 edition of the form, so confirm the current version on sba.gov.


- **Choose a license:** You want the guaranty and direct credit control, and can carry SBA exams and capital.
- **Choose a broker or platform model:** You want to offer SBA loans to your customers without becoming a lender.


Lendflow is a loan broker and platform; it does not lend and is not an SBA-approved LSP. Platforms use Data Orchestration and decline waterfalls to route SBA applications to lending partners through widgets, landing pages, and APIs.


Compare partner economics in our guide to[SBA broker referral programs](https://www.lendflow.com/post/sba-lender-broker-referral-programs-how-they-work-and-how-to-win) .


### Key Takeaways and Next Steps


Knowing how to become an SBA lender means passing regulatory, capital, and operational tests at once. Use this checklist before you call your district office.


- **Regulator:** Confirm a federal regulator, an SBA-satisfactory state regulator, or SBA supervises you.
- **Capital:** Document adequately capitalized status or the SBLC, Community Advantage, or NFRL minimum.
- **Policies:** Write commercially reasonable credit, servicing, and liquidation policies.
- **Systems:** Line up CAFS and E-Tran access, decisioning, and document workflows.
- **Performance plan:** Track Risk Rating drivers such as default, purchase, and loss rates.

### FAQs


### What is the SBA and what loan programs can approved lenders offer?


The U.S. Small Business Administration mostly guarantees loans that approved lenders make, rather than lending directly. Its programs include 7(a) loans, such as SBA Express with a 50% guaranty and $500,000 cap, plus 504 loans.


### What is the difference between an SBLC and a bank SBA lender?


An SBLC is supervised and examined solely by SBA, while a bank answers to its federal or state banking regulator. Banks meet capital rules by being adequately capitalized; SBLCs must hold the greater of $5 million or 10% of their loan share.


### What is the 20% rule for SBA loans?


Holders of at least 20% ownership generally must guarantee an SBA loan, per 13 CFR 120.160. SBA, or a lender using delegated authority, may require others to give full or limited guarantees.


### What types of capital count toward SBLC minimum capital?


Under 13 CFR 120.471, SBLC capital can include common stock, noncumulative perpetual preferred stock, additional paid-in capital, and retained earnings. Nonprofits can count unrestricted net assets, and LLCs or LPs can count contributions not repayable at a set time.


### How do you become a funding broker instead of a direct SBA lender?


Operate as a Referral Agent or Lender Service Provider under agreements with SBA lenders, with no SBA license required. Disclose agent fees on SBA Form 159 and avoid contingency fees, which SBA does not allow.
